paragraphs: Aligning two images requires estimating how locations in one image correspond to locations in the other. Earlier neural approaches predict parameters for a predefined transformation model. The paper argues that these compact models can be too restrictive when the actual deformation is complicated: learning the parameters cannot overcome limits in the transformation family itself.

Arbicon-Net instead predicts a dense displacement field directly, describing how positions should move across the image. The network is trained end to end and learns transformations from examples for use on previously unseen image pairs. A central theoretical result is that its predicted displacement function is spatially continuous and smooth without requiring additional penalty terms to enforce those properties.

The authors evaluate semantic alignment using synthetic and real images under several experimental settings. They report better identification of corresponding image locations than previous alignment techniques. The contribution therefore combines greater flexibility in representing deformation with a stated smoothness guarantee, alongside empirical evidence that this combination improves correspondence estimation in the tested settings.
neurips-2019-arbicon-net-arbitrary-conti.tldr: Arbicon-Net directly learns dense image transformations with guaranteed spatial smoothness and improves correspondence estimation in reported alignment experiments.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes more complicated when two players pursue competing objectives, because each player's update changes the problem facing the other. Alternating gradient descent can consequently oscillate or diverge. This paper introduces competitive gradient descent, an algorithm for numerically finding Nash equilibria that incorporates the interaction between players into the update itself.

Each step solves for the Nash equilibrium of a regularized, bilinear local approximation to the game. The authors compare this construction with approaches based on optimism and consensus, using both analysis and numerical experiments. For locally convex-concave zero-sum games, they establish exponential local convergence. They also report stability and convergence properties that remain robust to strong player interactions without adjusting the step size.

Experiments extend the investigation to problems outside the convex-concave setting. Existing methods exhibit interaction-related instability and divergence, while the authors observe no divergence for their algorithm in those experiments. Larger usable steps also reduce the number of model evaluations needed for convergence. These observations complement the local theorem; they do not constitute a universal convergence guarantee for arbitrary games.
neurips-2019-competitive-gradient-descen.tldr: Competitive gradient descent accounts for both players in each update, providing local convergence guarantees and improved empirical stability in competitive games.

paragraphs: Facial landmark detection involves locating a set of points whose positions are geometrically related. A prediction can therefore be judged both by the placement of individual points and by whether their arrangement is consistent. The paper argues that existing deep learning methods, despite strong performance, do not explicitly represent these dependencies and consequently struggle to preserve landmark geometry under difficult conditions.

The proposed method combines a deep convolutional network with a conditional random field. This brings image-based prediction together with a structured model of relationships among landmarks. The purpose is to make those relationships part of the prediction process, so that the model explicitly accounts for how landmark positions depend on one another.

The authors report superior performance over existing leading facial landmark methods, with particularly improved generalization on challenging datasets containing large pose changes and occlusion. These findings support the value of explicitly modeling facial structure when visual evidence becomes difficult to interpret. The stated result concerns performance on those evaluations, where preserving relationships among points accompanies better landmark detection.
neurips-2019-deep-structured-prediction-.tldr: Combining a convolutional network with a conditional random field improves facial landmark detection by explicitly modeling relationships among landmark positions.

paragraphs: A highly accurate model can still be difficult to understand. This paper proposes explaining a trained model through a symbolic metamodel: a surrogate expressed as a compact mathematical formula. Because the formula uses recognizable functions and supports symbolic manipulation, it provides a form that people can inspect and analyze when trying to understand predictions.

The technical challenge is finding a useful formula without specifying its functional form too narrowly in advance. The authors parameterize their surrogates using Meijer G-functions, a broad mathematical family whose different parameter settings reduce to many familiar functions. This representation permits gradient-based optimization while allowing the search to cover varied functional forms with relatively few prior assumptions.

The paper presents this symbolic representation as a common foundation for interpretation. It states that common global explanations, concerning overall model behavior, and local explanations, concerning particular predictions, can be derived analytically from the metamodel. The resulting explanations describe the trained model through its surrogate, making the symbolic expression the central object from which multiple kinds of interpretation follow.
neurips-2019-demystifying-black-box-mode.tldr: Symbolic metamodels explain trained models through optimized mathematical expressions from which global and local explanations can be derived.

paragraphs: Goal-oriented reinforcement learning can provide very little feedback when rewards depend on reaching a specified target. An agent may gather many experiences without receiving a useful success signal. Hindsight Experience Replay helps by reinterpreting past experience using imagined goals, creating an implicit progression of learning opportunities from what the agent has already done.

This paper introduces Hindsight Goal Generation to improve the choice of those goals. Its framework generates goals that are achievable in the near term while also having potential to guide the agent toward the actual target over the longer term. The key consideration is therefore both immediate feasibility and relevance to the eventual objective.

The authors evaluate the approach on several robotic manipulation tasks and report substantial gains in sample efficiency over the original hindsight replay method. This means the reported improvement concerns how effectively the agent learns from its experience. The findings support goal generation as an important part of addressing sparse rewards, with intermediate goals serving as useful learning opportunities on the way toward the desired task.
neurips-2019-exploration-via-hindsight-g.tldr: Hindsight Goal Generation improves sample efficiency in tested robotic tasks by choosing attainable intermediate goals with potential to support the final objective.

paragraphs: Belief propagation performs probabilistic inference by passing messages through a graph. Its behavior is well understood on trees, but cycles make convergence much harder to analyze. Earlier positive results often rely on assumptions ensuring that distant variables have progressively weaker influence on each other, a property called decay of correlations.

This paper proves fast convergence under a different set of conditions. For ferromagnetic Ising models, in which neighboring variables prefer alignment, belief propagation reaches the global optimum of the Bethe free energy from a natural initialization, even on arbitrary graphs. The result permits long-range correlations and the presence of other, suboptimal fixed points, so neither phenomenon by itself rules out the stated convergence.

The authors also establish an analogous result for iterative mean-field equations. Both results are dimension-free in the stated sense that a constant number of iterations gives a good estimate of the corresponding free energy. The guarantee concerns these variational objectives under the specified model and initialization conditions; it does not assert that loopy belief propagation becomes exact probabilistic inference on every graph.
neurips-2019-fast-convergence-of-belief-.tldr: For ferromagnetic Ising models under a natural initialization, belief propagation quickly optimizes Bethe free energy even when long-range correlations persist.

paragraphs: Compressing a convolutional network does not automatically make its computations inexpensive. This paper addresses both storage and arithmetic by examining the weight distributions that remain after fine-grained pruning. Its focused quantization strategy adapts the numerical representation of weights to layers with different levels of sparsity, using power-of-two values.

Power-of-two weights allow multiplication to be replaced by cheaper bit shifts. The authors combine this quantization with lossless encoding to form a compression pipeline intended to reduce model size and inference cost while keeping accuracy losses small. The approach connects the statistical structure of pruned weights with the operations needed to execute the compressed network.

For ResNet-50, the paper reports an 18.08-fold compression ratio with a 0.24% loss in top-5 accuracy, outperforming existing compression methods. A fully compressed ResNet-18 also improves compression ratio and top-5 accuracy over compared quantization methods. Its hardware comparison reports fewer required logic gates at equal throughput, providing evidence that the representation offers implementation benefits as well as a smaller stored model.
neurips-2019-focused-quantization-for-sp.tldr: Focused quantization adapts power-of-two weight representations to pruned CNNs, reducing storage and arithmetic costs with small reported accuracy losses.

paragraphs: Blind demodulation seeks two unknown vectors when only their elementwise product is observed. This paper constrains each vector to be an output of a known deep generative model. Those generative priors give structure to a recovery problem in which the two unknown quantities otherwise interact multiplicatively.

The landscape analysis assumes expansive networks with random weight matrices and an output dimension at least on the order of the sum of the squared latent dimensions, up to logarithmic factors. Under these conditions, the authors identify descent directions outside small neighborhoods of four hyperbolic curves and characterize local maximizers. Together, these results restrict where other stationary points can occur.

Only one of the four curves corresponds to global minimizers, and nearby points have lower objective values than points near the spurious curves. The authors use this geometry to design a gradient descent scheme that exploits the objective-value distinction when seeking a global solution. Experiments show effective removal of synthetic distortions from MNIST images. The theoretical landscape conclusions remain tied to the specified generative-network and dimensional assumptions.
neurips-2019-global-guarantees-for-blind.tldr: Under explicit generative-network assumptions, the paper characterizes blind demodulation’s optimization landscape and develops a geometry-informed recovery algorithm.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior using a more manageable distribution. Its quality depends on whether that distribution can express the posterior's structure. Requiring an easily evaluated density restricts this flexibility, creating a tension between a rich approximation and an objective that can actually be computed and optimized.

The paper develops bounds that help resolve this tension for hierarchical variational distributions. It first introduces a family of upper bounds on marginal log-densities in latent-variable models. From these, it derives increasingly tight lower bounds on the standard evidence lower bound, which can itself be intractable for these richer distributions. This provides usable optimization objectives for more expressive posterior approximations.

The framework also unifies several existing approaches: Hierarchical Variational Models, Semi-Implicit Variational Inference, and Doubly Semi-Implicit Variational Inference emerge as special cases. The authors report superior performance in their experiments. The contribution is thus both a broader mathematical construction for handling difficult densities and empirical evidence that the resulting inference method can improve on the compared approaches.
neurips-2019-importance-weighted-hierarc.tldr: New variational bounds make richer hierarchical posterior approximations usable while unifying several existing inference methods.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform without deploying it to collect exploratory experience. This matters when exploration is expensive or infeasible. The paper studies the problem in both contextual bandits and reinforcement learning, focusing on how to combine strong statistical efficiency with stable and bounded estimates.

Existing estimators offer different advantages. Doubly robust methods have a local efficiency guarantee when their Q-functions are correctly specified, but misspecification can make them less efficient than importance sampling or its self-normalized form. They also lack the inherent stability and boundedness attributed to self-normalized importance sampling. Thus, one desirable statistical property does not automatically provide the others.

The authors introduce estimators based on empirical likelihood and state that they are always more efficient than importance sampling, self-normalized importance sampling, and doubly robust estimation, while retaining the self-normalized method's stability and boundedness properties. They also organize existing estimators by their properties. Empirical studies suggest practical advantages, complementing the theoretical guarantees rather than replacing them with an exclusively experimental comparison.
neurips-2019-intrinsically-efficient-sta.tldr: Empirical-likelihood estimators combine stated efficiency improvements over common off-policy estimators with the stability and boundedness of self-normalized importance sampling.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers the behavior of a large trained network into a smaller student. The paper focuses on cases where the original training data cannot be accessed, including settings involving confidential or private information. This removes the examples normally used to expose the teacher's useful knowledge during the transfer process.

The difficulty is that a trained network's knowledge is concentrated in a narrow portion of the input space. Merely having the network does not supply representative examples from that region. KegNet addresses this problem using generative networks to extract knowledge from the trained model and produce artificial data points that substitute for the missing training examples.

Those generated examples provide the data used for distillation into a student. The authors report that KegNet outperforms all baselines in their data-free distillation experiments. The stated contribution is a way to perform knowledge transfer without observable training data, with experimental support for the usefulness of the generated replacements. It establishes an alternative source of distillation examples when direct access to the original data is unavailable.
neurips-2019-knowledge-extraction-with-n.tldr: KegNet generates artificial examples from a trained network to support knowledge distillation when original training data are unavailable.

paragraphs: In a contextual bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses an action using the context currently available and learns from the resulting reward. This paper studies the harder case where rewards arrive after unknown, random delays. Decisions must continue at every time step even though feedback from earlier choices may still be missing.

The authors develop Delayed UCB, an algorithm that adapts upper-confidence-bound exploration to generalized linear contextual bandits with delayed feedback. The exploration principle uses uncertainty when choosing actions, and the proposed adaptation accounts for the delayed setting. They establish regret bounds under several assumptions about delays, giving theoretical control over the performance cost of learning in these circumstances.

For the special case of linear contextual bandits, a further modification yields a tighter regret bound under the same delay assumptions. The results show that UCB-style methods can be made robust to delayed rewards within the analyzed settings. This is relevant to the recommendation applications highlighted by the paper, where choices may need to be made before previous outcomes become available.
neurips-2019-learning-in-generalized-lin.tldr: Delayed UCB adapts contextual-bandit exploration to randomly delayed rewards, with regret guarantees under several delay assumptions.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to prepare a model to learn new tasks quickly. Meta-curvature extends model-agnostic meta-learning by learning how to transform the gradients used during adaptation. The transformation is trained so that the resulting updates generalize better to a new task, making the update rule itself part of what is learned across tasks.

Representing interactions among many model parameters can require a large curvature matrix. To make the approach suitable for large neural networks, the authors decompose that matrix into smaller matrices. A sequence of tensor products captures parameter dependencies through this more manageable representation, allowing the learned transformation to account for relationships among parameters.

Across several few-shot learning tasks and datasets, the paper reports substantial improvements over earlier MAML variants and performance exceeding recent leading methods, without task-specific techniques or architectures. It also observes faster convergence during meta-training and provides an analysis explaining improved generalization from the learned curvature. Together, these findings support learning the geometry of adaptation as a useful addition to learning a model's initial parameters.
neurips-2019-meta-curvature-dac99d5979.tldr: Meta-curvature learns structured gradient transformations that improve few-shot adaptation and generalization in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Event sequences often contain interactions: one event can make another more or less likely. Standard Hawkes processes efficiently model mutually excitatory effects, but richer nonlinear variants can require discrete-time approximations for estimation. The paper argues that those approximations may compromise the quality of generated event sequences, even when more complex interactions can be represented.

The authors introduce a Bayesian point-process family with a nonlinear component that captures both excitation and inhibition in continuous time. They derive a fully Bayesian inference algorithm using Polya-Gamma augmentation and Poisson thinning. These mathematical tools support inference for the proposed model while preserving its continuous-time treatment of event occurrence.

Evaluation uses recordings of neuronal spikes from both single neurons and multiple neurons. The model generates biologically plausible spike trains while maintaining competitive predictive likelihoods, a combination the authors contrast with existing point-process models. This distinction matters because assigning good probabilities to observed data and generating realistic new sequences are different aspects of model quality. The reported results support the proposed approach on both fronts.
neurips-2019-mutually-regressive-point-p.tldr: A nonlinear Bayesian point-process model captures excitation and inhibition in continuous time and generates plausible neuronal spike trains with competitive predictive likelihoods.

paragraphs: Some time series evolve smoothly between events but change abruptly when an event occurs. Modeling either component alone misses part of that behavior. This paper develops a data-driven way to learn both the continuous motion and the jumps when the equations describing them are not already known.

Neural Jump Stochastic Differential Equations extend Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with a stochastic process term for discrete events. The resulting latent trajectory is continuous between events and can jump at event times. Event intensity depends on the latent state, connecting the system's current internal condition to the likelihood of another event occurring.

The authors use this construction to model temporal point processes and demonstrate predictive capabilities on synthetic and real marked-event datasets. Their evaluations include classical processes such as Hawkes processes, Stack Overflow awards, medical records, and earthquake monitoring. The contribution is a unified representation of evolving state and abrupt event-driven changes, with predictive demonstrations across several kinds of event sequences rather than a model confined to only continuous dynamics.
neurips-2019-neural-jump-stochastic-diff.tldr: Neural Jump Stochastic Differential Equations learn continuous dynamics together with random event-driven jumps for modeling temporal event sequences.

paragraphs: Inferring an opponent's objective becomes harder when that opponent can deliberately hide it. This paper introduces non-cooperative inverse reinforcement learning to represent that strategic problem. It considers two agents with completely opposed objectives, where only one knows the true objective function and the other must learn about it through interaction.

The formal model is a zero-sum Markov game with incomplete information on one side. This information structure allows the multistage game to be expressed recursively through single-stage games. One recursion determines the game's value and the informed player's equilibrium strategy. A second recursion, obtained from an auxiliary dual game, provides the less informed player's strategy.

Building on these recursions, the authors develop a computationally tractable algorithm for approximately finding equilibrium strategies. Numerical simulations in a cybersecurity setting demonstrate benefits over an existing multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning formalism. The approach matters because behavior is treated as strategically chosen under unequal information: an observed action may serve both the opponent's objective and its effort to keep that objective concealed.
neurips-2019-non-cooperative-inverse-rei.tldr: Non-cooperative inverse reinforcement learning models objective inference against a strategically deceptive opponent and approximately computes both players’ equilibrium strategies.

paragraphs: A classifier with a rejection option can decline to assign a label when doing so helps avoid a critical mistake. This paper asks whether training methods for that choice are calibrated to the Bayes-optimal solution. Here, calibration concerns whether the training objective aligns with the best classification-and-rejection decision rule.

The authors first examine joint training of a classifier and a separate rejector, an approach that performs strongly for binary classification. They derive a general calibration condition for the multiclass case. Their analysis suggests that satisfying this condition with general loss functions is difficult, showing that the favorable binary situation does not straightforwardly carry over to multiple classes.

They then study rejection based on confidence scores. Extending earlier work beyond a specific class of losses, they propose rejection criteria for more general losses and guarantee calibration for this approach. Experiments validate the relevance of the theoretical findings. The contribution identifies a difficulty in one training formulation and provides a theoretically supported route for deciding when a multiclass classifier should abstain.
neurips-2019-on-the-calibration-of-multi.tldr: The paper analyzes calibration difficulties for jointly trained multiclass rejectors and provides calibrated confidence-based rejection criteria for more general losses.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional networks face different computational problems depending on their representation. Dense voxel grids become expensive as resolution increases because memory and computation grow cubically. Point-based networks avoid that dense representation, but irregular access to sparse data can consume much of their execution time instead of useful feature extraction.

Point-Voxel CNN combines the two representations. It stores the input as points to control memory consumption and performs convolutions in voxels to improve memory locality. The design connects representation choice to hardware efficiency: compact point storage and more regular convolutional access address separate sources of cost.

On semantic and part segmentation datasets, PVCNN reports higher accuracy than a voxel baseline with tenfold lower GPU memory use, and an average sevenfold measured speedup over leading point-based models while also improving accuracy. A narrower version achieves twice PointNet's speed with higher accuracy on the reported segmentation benchmarks. Replacing components in Frustrum PointNet with PVConv also improves detection over Frustrum PointNet++, with a reported 2.4% average mAP gain, 1.5-fold speedup, and reduced GPU memory use.
neurips-2019-point-voxel-cnn-for-efficie.tldr: PVCNN combines point storage with voxel convolutions to improve accuracy, speed, and memory efficiency in reported 3D learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network involves optimizing a game, and noisy gradient estimates can change whether the optimization converges. This paper studies that noise directly. It shows that stochastic gradients can prevent convergence for standard game-optimization methods even in cases where their batch counterparts converge, making gradient noise a substantive obstacle to training.

The proposed stochastic variance-reduced extragradient algorithm, abbreviated SVRE, addresses that obstacle by reducing variance within an extragradient method. The authors establish improved convergence rates over previous results for a large class of games. This theoretical contribution connects the treatment of stochastic noise to stronger optimization guarantees for that class.

In experiments on MNIST, SVRE behaves similarly to a batch method while requiring less computation. The authors also observe more stable GAN training on standard datasets. These findings suggest that reducing noise can retain useful behavior associated with batch optimization while lowering its computational cost. The empirical stability results complement the game-level analysis, rather than asserting convergence for every possible GAN training problem.
neurips-2019-reducing-noise-in-gan-train.tldr: SVRE reduces stochastic gradient noise in game optimization, improving theoretical convergence rates and empirical GAN training stability.

paragraphs: Neural inference on encrypted inputs must work within the operations supported efficiently by the encryption scheme. Earlier leveled homomorphic approaches approximate activations and pooling with polynomials. The paper identifies the cost and accumulated approximation errors of these operations as obstacles to accurate, deeper networks.

SHE uses a leveled TFHE scheme suited to binary operations to implement ReLU activations and max pooling. Logarithmic quantization replaces expensive encrypted multiplications with cheaper shifts, while a mixed-bitwidth accumulator speeds accumulation. These components have small multiplicative depth, allowing the system to support architectures with more convolutional and activation layers.

The design therefore addresses both the behavior of the neural network and the expense of executing it under encryption. On MNIST and CIFAR-10, the authors report state-of-the-art inference accuracy and latency reductions ranging from 76.21% to 94.23% relative to prior leveled-encryption CNNs. These results provide experimental support for choosing network arithmetic and encryption operations together when building an accurate, efficient encrypted inference system.
neurips-2019-she-a-fast-and-accurate-dee.tldr: SHE combines encryption-friendly activations, pooling, shifts, and accumulation to enable deeper encrypted networks with improved reported accuracy and latency.

paragraphs: The alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, is widely used because it combines simplicity, flexibility, and efficiency. Even so, improving its optimization performance remains an important problem. This paper examines acceleration through the geometry of ADMM's trajectory: the path formed by its successive optimization iterates.

The authors use that geometric perspective to discuss limitations of existing inertial acceleration methods. Their approach makes the behavior of the underlying iteration central to understanding acceleration. They then present and analyze an adaptive acceleration scheme for ADMM, connecting the proposed improvement to the trajectory properties investigated in the paper.

Numerical experiments cover problems from image processing, statistics, and machine learning, and demonstrate advantages for the proposed scheme. The evidence therefore combines analysis of the method's behavior with evaluations across several application areas. The main contribution is a geometry-informed approach to improving an established optimizer, together with an account of why current inertial acceleration has limitations and a proposed adaptive alternative.
neurips-2019-trajectory-of-alternating-d.tldr: The paper studies ADMM’s trajectory geometry to analyze inertial acceleration limits and develop an adaptive acceleration scheme with demonstrated numerical advantages.

paragraphs: Physiological time-series models often combine convolutional layers with recurrent layers to capture temporal relationships. The authors report that recurrent systems can be difficult to optimize and may need task-specific adjustments. U-Time addresses this practical difficulty with a fully feed-forward architecture developed for segmenting sleep recordings.

The model adapts the U-Net architecture to temporal signals. It accepts sequences of arbitrary length and produces class-label sequences at a chosen temporal scale. Its mechanism implicitly classifies individual time points, then combines those classifications over fixed intervals to generate the final predictions. This connects detailed signal interpretation to the interval-level labels required by the task.

The authors evaluate sleep-stage classification across a large collection of EEG datasets. In every evaluated case, U-Time matches or exceeds the compared leading deep learning models, with more robust training and no architecture or hyperparameter changes across tasks. The result supports fully convolutional modeling as an effective approach to these sleep-staging evaluations, with practical benefits in how consistently the model can be trained.
neurips-2019-u-time-a-fully-convolutiona.tldr: U-Time uses fully convolutional temporal segmentation to achieve strong sleep-staging results with robust training across the evaluated EEG datasets.

paragraphs: Probabilistic formulations let reinforcement learning use tools such as variational inference, but their design affects which policies can be learned. This paper identifies difficulties in earlier frameworks involving mode capture, deterministic policies, and analysis with function approximation. VIREL provides a probabilistic framework that uses a parameterized action-value function to summarize future dynamics.

The framework uses a mode-seeking form of KL divergence and naturally accommodates deterministic optimal policies. It also separates policy optimization from value-function optimization into alternating steps. Applying variational expectation-maximization makes that relationship explicit: policy improvement corresponds to the expectation step, while policy evaluation corresponds to the maximization step.

From this formulation, the authors derive a family of actor-critic algorithms, including a method for adaptive exploration. Algorithms in that family outperform leading soft-value-function methods in several evaluated domains. The contribution links a theoretical account of reinforcement learning as inference to concrete training procedures, showing how choices in the inference formulation can guide both policy learning and value estimation.
neurips-2019-virel-a-variational-inferen.tldr: VIREL formulates actor-critic learning as variational expectation-maximization and derives algorithms with adaptive exploration and strong reported empirical performance.

paragraphs: Connections between overparameterized neural networks and kernel methods explain some neural-network learning behavior, but leave open whether networks can provably do better. This paper establishes such a separation for a particular class of functions. Its results are distribution-free, meaning the learning guarantee does not require assumptions about the input distribution.

The learnable class includes functions represented by three-layer residual networks with smooth activations. Within that class, the authors identify simple functions for which neural networks achieve much lower test error than any kernel method using the same number of training examples. The comparison includes neural tangent kernels, making the result directly relevant to kernel-based accounts of neural learning.

The proposed explanation is hierarchical learning across multiple layers, which can reduce the examples needed compared with the one-shot learning behavior of kernel methods. The paper also proves a computational complexity advantage over other learning methods, including linear regression with arbitrary feature mappings. These are separations for the studied function class, rather than a claim that residual networks outperform kernels on every learning problem.
neurips-2019-what-can-resnet-learn-effic.tldr: The paper proves that residual networks can efficiently learn a function class containing examples where they generalize substantially better than any kernel method.

paragraphs: Adaptive momentum methods use past gradients to adjust both update directions and learning rates. That information is unavailable in black-box optimization when explicit gradients cannot be obtained. ZO-AdaMM extends adaptive momentum to this gradient-free setting, bringing an adaptive optimization approach to problems accessible through their outputs.

For convex and nonconvex optimization, the authors show a convergence rate roughly worse than the first-order counterpart by a factor on the order of the square root of the problem dimension. Their analysis also explains the importance of Mahalanobis distance to convergence and contributes toward understanding adaptive learning rates in constrained nonconvex problems. The dimensional factor makes the theoretical cost of losing direct gradient access explicit.

The paper demonstrates the method through per-image and universal adversarial attacks on black-box neural networks. In ImageNet experiments, ZO-AdaMM reaches high-accuracy solutions substantially faster than six compared leading zeroth-order optimization methods. These experiments support the practical value of adaptive momentum without explicit gradients, alongside an analysis of its convergence behavior and dimensional dependence.
neurips-2019-zo-adamm-zeroth-order-adapt.tldr: ZO-AdaMM extends adaptive momentum to black-box optimization, with convergence analysis and faster reported performance on adversarial-attack experiments.
